items.title: Composition & Vertical Structure of the Atmosphere
items.body:
## Composition

- Dry air is **~78% nitrogen** (diluent, inert) and **~21% oxygen** (respiration, combustion); the rest is **argon (0.93%)**, **CO₂ (0.03%)** and traces.
- **Water vapour** (0–5% by volume) decreases from equator to poles; it is a greenhouse regulator and the source of all condensation forms.
- **CO₂** absorbs and re-radiates terrestrial radiation (greenhouse gas); **ozone** absorbs UV; **dust/salt particles** scatter light (blue sky, red sunsets) and act as hygroscopic nuclei.

## Vertical layers (bottom to top)

| Layer | Extent | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| Troposphere | ~13 km (16 eq., 6 poles) | All weather; lapse rate 6.5°C/1000 m; ends at tropopause |
| Stratosphere | up to 50 km | Ozone layer (15–30 km); stable, ideal for flying |
| Mesosphere | 50–80 km | Meteorites burn up; coldest at mesopause (−80°C) |
| Thermosphere | above 80 km | Temperature rises fast; ionosphere reflects radio waves; ISS |
| Exosphere | outermost | Very rarefied; H and He escape to space |
keyPoints: Dry air ≈ 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.93% argon, 0.03% CO₂.
Water vapour (0–5%) is the source of clouds, fog, dew, rain and a greenhouse regulator.
Troposphere holds all weather; normal lapse rate is 6.5°C per 1000 m.
Ozone layer sits in the stratosphere (15–30 km) and absorbs UV radiation.
The ionosphere (in the thermosphere) reflects radio waves; meteorites burn in the mesosphere.
items.mnemonic: Layers upward: 'The Sun My Turtle Eats' = Troposphere, Stratosphere, Mesosphere, Thermosphere, Exosphere.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Climatology: Composition and Structure of Atmosphere

figure.caption: Troposphere → stratosphere (ozone) → mesosphere → thermosphere → exosphere.

items.title: Insolation, Heat Budget & Temperature
items.body:
## Insolation & albedo

- **Insolation** = incoming solar radiation received at the surface; greatest in the tropics, least at the poles.
- **Albedo** = fraction of incident radiation reflected back. Fresh snow and cloud tops have high albedo.

## Heat budget (of 100 units at top of atmosphere)

- **35 units reflected** back to space (the earth's albedo: 27 clouds + 2 ice/snow + 6 scatter/ground).
- **65 units absorbed**: 14 by the atmosphere, 51 by the surface.
- Earth re-radiates the 51 units as **long-wave terrestrial radiation** (17 direct to space + 34 to atmosphere).
- Outgoing 17 + 48 = **65 units** balances the incoming 65 → the earth neither warms nor cools overall.

## Temperature controls & inversion

- Controls: **latitude, altitude, distance from sea, air masses and ocean currents.**
- **Isotherms** join places of equal temperature.
- **Temperature inversion**: temperature rises with height (lapse rate reversed) — favoured by long, clear, calm winter nights; traps fog, smoke and dust; valley 'air drainage' inversions protect crops from frost.
keyPoints: Of incoming insolation, ~35 units are reflected (albedo) and 65 absorbed (14 atmosphere + 51 surface).
The heat budget balances: 65 units in = 65 units out, keeping global temperature steady.
Earth is heated indirectly from below by long-wave terrestrial radiation absorbed by CO₂/water vapour.
Temperature controls: latitude, altitude, distance from sea, air masses and ocean currents.
Temperature inversion (warm over cold) forms on clear, calm winter nights and traps fog/pollutants.
Cloud radiative effect depends on altitude: high thin clouds trap outgoing infrared and warm the surface, while low thick clouds reflect sunlight and cool it.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Climatology: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature

items.title: Pressure Belts & Planetary/Local Winds
items.body:
## Global pressure belts (equator → pole)

| Belt | Latitude | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| Equatorial low (ITCZ / doldrums) | 0° | Thermal; calm, rising air |
| Subtropical high (Horse latitudes) | ~30°N/S | Dynamic; descending air |
| Subpolar low | ~60°N/S | Dynamic; cyclonic storms |
| Polar high | 90°N/S | Thermal; cold dense air |

- Belts **shift with the apparent movement of the sun** (northward in June, southward in December) — the basis of seasonal winds and monsoons.

## Planetary winds

- **Trade winds** (30° → equator, NE/SE), **Westerlies** (30° → 60°), **Polar easterlies** (poles → 60°).
- Southern-hemisphere westerlies are the **Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Screaming Sixties** (little land to obstruct them).
- **Coriolis force** deflects winds right (N) and left (S); zero at the equator, maximum at poles.

## Local winds

| Wind | Character | Region |
|---|---|---|
| Loo | Hot, dry | N. India (May–June) |
| Foehn | Warm, dry | Leeward Alps |
| Chinook ('snow-eater') | Warm, dry | Rockies |
| Mistral | Cold | Rhone valley, France |
| Sirocco | Hot, dusty | Sahara → Mediterranean |
keyPoints: Four pressure belts: equatorial low, subtropical high (Horse latitudes), subpolar low, polar high.
Equatorial low and polar high are thermal; subtropical high and subpolar low are dynamic.
Planetary winds: trade winds, westerlies, polar easterlies, controlled by pressure belts.
SH westerlies = Roaring Forties/Furious Fifties/Screaming Sixties due to open ocean.
Loo (N. India hot), Chinook (Rockies warm), Mistral (France cold), Foehn (leeward Alps warm).
items.mnemonic: Warm descending winds warm the leeward: Foehn (Alps) & Chinook (Rockies) both melt snow.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Climatology: Atmospheric Circulation; Pressure and Winds

items.title: Cyclones — Tropical vs Temperate, Naming & AP Coast
items.body:
## Tropical cyclones

- Violent storms forming over **warm seas (SST > 27°C)**; called **Cyclones** (Indian Ocean), **Hurricanes** (Atlantic), **Typhoons** (W. Pacific), **Willy-willies** (W. Australia).
- Formation needs: SST > 27°C, **Coriolis force** (hence none near the equator), low vertical wind shear, a pre-existing low, and upper-level divergence.
- Structure: calm **eye** (subsiding air) → **eye wall** (strongest winds, torrential rain) → spiralling rain bands. Dissipates on landfall as moisture is cut off.

## Temperate (extratropical) cyclones

- Form along the **polar front** in mid/high latitudes; have a clear **frontal system**; move **west → east**; can form over land or sea.
- Tropical cyclones move **east → west**, form only over sea, and are more destructive.

## Naming & the AP coast

- **IMD** is one of six global **RSMCs**; it names north-Indian-Ocean cyclones under the **WMO/ESCAP** panel (8 members from 2000, +5 in 2018 = 13).
- The **Bay of Bengal** is far more cyclogenic than the Arabian Sea, so the **AP east coast (~974 km)** is highly cyclone-prone; peak season **Oct–Nov** (post-monsoon), with a pre-monsoon spell too.
- **Cyclone Hudhud (Oct 2014)** made landfall near **Visakhapatnam**, causing severe damage — a key AP case study.
keyPoints: Tropical cyclones need SST > 27°C and the Coriolis force; none form within ~5° of the equator.
Structure: calm eye, violent eye wall, spiralling rain bands; they weaken on landfall.
Tropical cyclones move E→W (sea only); temperate cyclones move W→E along the polar front with fronts.
IMD (an RSMC) names north-Indian-Ocean cyclones under WMO/ESCAP (13 member nations).
Bay of Bengal > Arabian Sea in cyclones; AP east coast peak season is Oct–Nov; Hudhud (2014) hit Visakhapatnam.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Climatology: Air Masses and Cyclone; India Meteorological Department (IMD)

items.title: Indian Monsoon Mechanism, ENSO & IOD
items.body:
## Mechanism of the Indian monsoon

- The monsoon is a **seasonal reversal of winds** driven by **differential land–sea heating** and the seasonal migration of the **ITCZ (monsoon trough)**.
- In summer, intense heating of NW India creates a **thermal low**; the ITCZ shifts north, drawing the moisture-laden **south-west (summer) monsoon** across the equator.
- Aids: the **cross-equatorial Somali jet**, the **tropical easterly jet**, and the withdrawal of the subtropical westerly jet north of the Himalayas.

## SW vs NE monsoon

| Feature | South-west (summer) | North-east (retreating) |
|---|---|---|
| Period | June–September | October–December |
| Onset | Kerala ~1 June | After SW withdrawal |
| Rain area | Most of India | Coastal AP & Tamil Nadu |

- **Burst** = sudden onset of heavy monsoon rain; a **break** = a dry spell within the season.
- The **retreating (NE) monsoon** gives coastal Andhra Pradesh much of its rain in Oct–Dec.

## ENSO & IOD

- **El Niño** (warm central-east Pacific) → generally a **weaker** Indian monsoon; **La Niña** → generally a **good** monsoon. Together with the **Southern Oscillation** this is **ENSO**.
- **Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)**: a **positive IOD** (warm western Indian Ocean) generally **favours** monsoon rain and can offset an El Niño year.
keyPoints: The monsoon is a seasonal wind reversal driven by land–sea heating and the seasonal shift of the ITCZ.
SW monsoon: June–Sept, onsets over Kerala ~1 June, waters most of India; aided by the Somali & easterly jets.
NE (retreating) monsoon: Oct–Dec, brings most rain to coastal AP and Tamil Nadu.
'Burst' = sudden monsoon onset; 'break' = a dry spell within the season.
El Niño weakens and La Niña strengthens the monsoon; a positive IOD favours rainfall.
The IOD is the SST difference between the tropical western Indian Ocean and the south-eastern Indian Ocean (near Indonesia) — NOT the eastern Pacific; a positive IOD can offset an El Niño.
items.mnemonic: SW = 'Summer, Wet, whole country'; NE = 'Now East coast (AP/TN) in winter'.
items.source: India Meteorological Department (IMD); NCERT India — Physical Environment (Climate)

items.title: Condensation, Precipitation & Köppen Classification
items.body:
## Humidity & condensation

- **Relative humidity** = actual vapour ÷ capacity at that temperature (%); **dew point** = temperature at which saturation occurs.
- Forms of condensation depend on whether the dew point is above or below freezing: **dew** (above 0°C), **frost** (at/below 0°C), plus **fog, mist, clouds**. Fog + smoke = **smog**.

## Types of precipitation (by lifting mechanism)

| Type | Cause | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Convectional | Surface heating, rising warm air | Equatorial afternoons |
| Orographic | Air forced up a mountain; rain shadow to leeward | Western Ghats |
| Cyclonic/frontal | Converging air / warm air over cold along a front | Temperate cyclones |

## Köppen's climate classification (1918)

- Empirical scheme linking **climate to vegetation**; five main groups + highland:
  - **A** Tropical humid (Af wet, Am monsoon, Aw wet-and-dry)
  - **B** Dry (BS steppe, BW desert; h hot, k cold)
  - **C** Warm temperate (Cs Mediterranean, Cfa/Cfb humid, Cwa dry-winter)
  - **D** Cold snow-forest (Df, Dw)
  - **E** Polar (ET tundra, EF ice-cap)
  - **H** Highland
- Four groups are temperature-based; **B is precipitation-based**. Most of India is **Am/Aw**, with **Cwa** over the north plains and **BW/BS** in the north-west.
keyPoints: Dew forms with dew point above 0°C; frost at/below 0°C; fog + smoke = smog.
Precipitation types: convectional (heating), orographic (mountains), cyclonic/frontal (converging air).
Köppen (1918) links climate to vegetation; groups A, B, C, D, E and highland H.
Four Köppen groups are temperature-based; group B is precipitation-based.
Af = tropical wet, Am = tropical monsoon, BWh = hot desert, Cs = Mediterranean; India is mainly Am/Aw.
items.source: APPSC GK PDF — Climatology: Water in the Atmosphere; Köppen's Scheme of Classification of Climate

items.title: Air Masses & Fronts
items.body:
## Air masses

An **air mass** is a large body of air with fairly uniform temperature and humidity, acquired over a calm, uniform **source region** (oceans, snowfields, deserts). It is classified by source:

| Symbol | Source | Character |
|---|---|---|
| cP / cA | Continental polar / Arctic (Siberia, N. Canada) | Cold, dry |
| mP | Maritime polar (cold high-latitude oceans) | Cold, moist |
| cT | Continental tropical (Sahara, deserts) | Hot, dry |
| mT | Maritime tropical (warm oceans, Gulf) | Warm, moist |

An air mass is **modified** along its track — e.g. cold air moving over a warm sea gains heat and moisture and becomes unstable.

## Fronts

A **front** is the sloping boundary where two contrasting air masses meet along the **polar front**.

| Front | Slope | Weather |
|---|---|---|
| **Cold** | Steep | Warm air forced up sharply → cumulonimbus, brief heavy squally rain, then a sharp temperature drop and clearing |
| **Warm** | Gentle | Warm air glides up slowly → cirrus→cirrostratus→altostratus→nimbostratus, prolonged steady rain, then warming |
| **Occluded** | Complex | Fast cold front overtakes the warm front, lifting the warm sector aloft; marks the **dying stage** of a mid-latitude cyclone |
| **Stationary** | — | Neither air mass advances; persistent dull, cloudy weather |

## Temperate (mid-latitude) cyclone life cycle

Frontogenesis → mature (open warm sector between cold and warm fronts) → **occlusion** → dissipation.
keyPoints: Air mass = large body of air with uniform temperature/humidity from a uniform source region.
Classification: cP/cA cold-dry, mP cold-moist, cT hot-dry, mT warm-moist.
Air masses are modified along their track (cold air over warm sea becomes warm, moist, unstable).
Cold front: steep slope, cumulonimbus, brief violent rain, then temperature falls.
Warm front: gentle slope, cloud sequence cirrus→nimbostratus, prolonged steady rain, then warming.
Occluded front forms when a cold front overtakes a warm front — the dissipating stage of a temperate cyclone.
Stationary front: neither air mass can displace the other.
items.mnemonic: First letter = moisture (c=dry continental, m=moist maritime); second = temperature (P/A cold, T hot).
items.source: NCERT — Fundamentals of Physical Geography (Air Masses & Fronts); local APPSC GK PDF — Climatology: Air Masses and Cyclone
